title: Platform overview
description: Scope, compatibility and the development stack.

sections.heading: Platform overview
sections.text: kaiHEN Platform and Compatibility Research snapshot: November 13, 2026, America/New_York. This guide concerns native Switch 2 homebrew applications built with the public ouncebrew stack. Its practical baseline is a pinned kaiHEN runtime, the ounce-devkit toolchain, libounce, and an application that can enter and exit cleanly before larger features are added.

sections.heading: What kaiHEN provides
sections.text: What kaiHEN provides kaiHEN describes itself as a homebrew environment and minimal custom firmware. It supplies resident loader and service components rather than a complete application framework. The development repository points existing libnx applications toward libounce and OpenGL or Vulkan. Access is broad enough to include system storage; an application should therefore treat every write target as an explicit product decision. kaiHEN project overview The stack has several independently versioned parts: Part Developer role Typical output or interface --- --- --- kaiHEN RO and HEN Load programs and provide the homebrew environment Native services and homebrew sessions ounce-hbloader Run sequential NROs in a native game process The game main module ounce-hbmenu Select and launch applications hbmenu.nro libounce Supply libnx-style runtime and operating-system wrappers Headers and static libraries OunceVK Supply Vulkan and EGL/OpenGL rendering Static driver libraries libkaihen Expose HEN, JIT and plugin interfaces kaihen.h and supporting libraries ounce-devkit Assemble build rules, libraries and examples A devkitPro overlay The library and compiler arrangement is significant: the devkit layers Switch 2 support over devkitPro rather than replacing its entire toolchain. Development kit installation and usage

sections.heading: Firmware and acquisition scope
sections.text: Firmware and acquisition scope Application development and acquiring an initial homebrew environment are separate dependencies. A working game exploit alone does not establish that a native NRO loader or all required services are available. Its release-path assumptions therefore need reconciliation before using it with the public archive. A firmware-independent application source tree still needs a working runtime on the target console. sections.heading: Source compatibility and binary compatibility
sections.text: Source compatibility and binary compatibility libounce adds a platform record to linked programs. Its NRO definitions identify Switch 1 and Switch 2 separately; a traditional libnx program lacks that record. NRO platform identity record hbmenu warns before launching programs that were not built with the Switch 2 devkit. Switch 2 menu usage and rendering The useful porting question is consequently: “Which source-level interfaces does this application use?” A portable C parser is easier to reuse than code issuing device ioctls or assuming a particular display-buffer layout. An old .nro filename is not a compatibility guarantee. A successful link is also insufficient: graphics, services, audio, file access and shutdown each have observable behavior to verify.

sections.heading: Choosing a first project
sections.text: Choosing a first project The lowest-friction first projects are a diagnostic utility, a small SDL2 application, an existing libnx application with ordinary file access, or a renderer with a modest OpenGL ES feature set. This is an engineering assessment based on interface breadth, not a claim that every application in those categories already works. An emulator, streaming client or large game engine introduces several coupled systems. Start it as a sequence of milestones: native startup, input, files, one frame, sound, workload, repeated exit, and sustained use. A project depending on a privileged service should prove that service independently before importing a large UI or renderer. The community homebrew list is useful for finding repositories such as OunceShell, RetroArch, Moonlight, mGBA and game ports. It is a project directory, not a test certificate for a particular release binary. Community application and plugin directory

sections.heading: Initial decision record
sections.text: Initial decision record Before choosing a framework, write down the application purpose, target firmware, acquisition route, runtime release, devkit version, rendering API, storage needs, network needs and exit behavior. Identify optional features that can be disabled when unavailable. This makes the first hardware result interpretable and turns later upstream changes into bounded updates. Continue with Runtime architecture and Toolchain and reproducible builds.

sections.heading: Set up the toolchain
sections.text: kaiHEN Toolchain and Reproducible Builds The development kit is an overlay on devkitPro. Reproducibility depends on selecting the Switch 2 headers and libraries before the original Switch libraries, recording the package versions, and rebuilding static dependencies when they change.

sections.heading: Make projects
sections.text: Make projects The central rules include is: Those rules set LIBNX to libounce, select the Switch 2 overlay first, and define __SWITCH2__ . They preserve the familiar -lnx spelling through the installed library arrangement. Switch 2 Make rules and library overlay Use $(SWITCH2_CPU) where the project's ARCH is defined. The inspected CPU flags are -mcpu=cortex-a78c+crypto ; copying a Switch 1 architecture setting later in a Makefile can override the intended target. Shared Switch 2 CPU flags Useful linking choices are: Feature Primary link selection Additional condition --- --- --- Ordinary native application -lnx with Switch 2 rules Correct include and library search order Small runtime using newlib malloc -lounce_core Deliberate allocator choice Vulkan -lvulkan before runtime Switch 2 driver overlay OpenGL or GLES through EGL -lEGL before runtime Use the overlay EGL headers kaiHEN JIT -lkaihen provider Inspect final link command Native plugin -lkaihen_plugin -lounce_core NSO startup conventions The allocator split is implemented in libounce's build. Runtime and allocator packaging OunceVK's packaging supplies linker scripts for the public graphics library names. Static graphics driver packaging

sections.heading: CMake, Meson and autotools
sections.text: CMake, Meson and autotools Source the environment before configuring: The CMake toolchain keeps CMAKE_SYSTEM_NAME as NintendoSwitch for existing project logic, changes NX_ROOT to libounce, and prioritizes Switch 2 packages. Its platform layer sets NINTENDO_SWITCH2 . Switch 2 CMake toolchain CMake platform flags and overlay Use separate build directories for Switch 1, Switch 2 and host builds. A cached find_package result can preserve the wrong graphics library even after environment variables change. For Meson or autotools, inspect their actual target, compiler, include directories and pkg-config output rather than assuming that sourcing a script proves correct configuration. The environment file exports architecture flags and the overlay prefixes. Cross-build environment variables

sections.heading: Build products and metadata
sections.text: Build products and metadata An ordinary application should retain its .elf and linker map alongside the distributable .nro . The reference Makefiles use nacptool and elf2nro to assemble application metadata and assets; setting up an NPDM JSON can instead switch the template into an ExeFS package path. Do not add such a JSON file casually to an NRO project. GLES example NRO build pipeline The plugin example demonstrates a smaller direct route: cross-compile a C file, link an ELF against the plugin runtime, then convert with elf2nso . Native plugin ELF and NSO build

sections.heading: Reproducibility record
sections.text: Reproducibility record Store the application commit, dirty-tree state, toolchain package inventory, devkit release, library source pins, container digest, compiler version, build command and output hashes. For shader-heavy programs, also record shader compiler versions and source hashes. A deterministic build needs stable inputs; a successful build merely needs inputs that happen to work. Inspect the full link command before debugging runtime symptoms. Search for /libnx paths that bypass libounce, the wrong libEGL.a , accidental host paths, old CPU flags and stale static libraries. Save that command in the build log. This single check often separates a platform porting issue from a dependency-selection error.

title: Build your first app
description: A native diagnostic, controller input and a clean return to hbmenu.

sections.heading: Build your first app
sections.text: kaiHEN First Application and Lifecycle The first useful application is a small native diagnostic: it should render something simple, obtain HEN status, respond to a controller button, and return to hbmenu. This gives a clear baseline before assets, network services or an engine obscure failures.

sections.heading: Recommended project structure
sections.text: Recommended project structure Keep application logic independent of console initialization. A parser, asset index, state machine or protocol codec should be testable on the host. Put platform calls behind a small layer so a hardware failure does not require rewriting the entire project. Use a current upstream example Makefile as the build foundation and change its title, author, target and source directories. The devkit's GLES and Vulkan examples demonstrate the native rules and output pipeline. GLES example NRO build pipeline Vulkan example build and metadata

sections.heading: Original diagnostic example
sections.text: Original diagnostic example The following is an illustrative application assembled for this research. It has not been cross-compiled or executed on a console. It uses declared libounce and libkaihen interfaces; hardware validation remains the next acceptance step. The console renderer is useful for diagnostics, while a production UI can use SDL2, EGL or Vulkan. The status calls and session ownership follow the client declarations. kaiHEN client API and handle ownership Pad helpers provide the controller aggregation and edge detection. Pad state and controller helpers libounce has a Switch 2 CPU framebuffer implementation behind the familiar display API. Switch 2 CPU framebuffer adaptation An IPC request succeeding does not imply initialization_result is zero. Display both values and gate features on the required protocol. If status fails, leave ordinary UI and exit controls functional so the application can still report a useful failure.

sections.heading: Initialization as a transaction
sections.text: Initialization as a transaction For larger programs, maintain explicit state for each completed initialization stage. Allocate only after its prerequisites are available. If a later step fails, unwind completed stages in reverse order. This ordering is a suggested design. Some applications need different dependencies, but the invariant remains: cleanup must know which resources were actually acquired. Do not call a close routine on an uninitialized structure merely because another platform tolerated it.

sections.heading: File and asset conventions
sections.text: File and asset conventions Use RomFS for immutable packaged assets and an application-specific SD directory for mutable state. romfsInit and romfsExit expose the packaged asset mount through the runtime. RomFS mount API For example, choose sdmc:/switch/myapp/ for settings and logs. This path is an application convention, not a kaiHEN-enforced sandbox. Keep user files separate from generated caches so a cleanup command can remove disposable data without touching valuable content. Treat file errors as normal outcomes: missing SD card, directory creation failure, incomplete file, full storage and unsupported format should produce a recoverable state. Keep the last valid configuration when a new one fails to parse.

sections.heading: Main-loop design
sections.text: Main-loop design Poll input and platform lifecycle events regularly. Move long file scans, network waits and decompression out of the render loop. Worker results should enter the UI through a bounded queue or a documented synchronization primitive. A worker must not directly mutate renderer-owned objects without the rendering API's threading rules being satisfied. Use frame elapsed time for animation and game simulation. Do not equate one iteration with 1/60 second. Docked output, display changes and stalled frames make that assumption fragile.

sections.heading: Shutdown contract
sections.text: Shutdown contract Stop accepting new work, notify workers, cancel or finish outstanding requests, join threads, stop audio, release graphics resources, flush and close files, close owned sessions and return from main . Teardown should tolerate a partially initialized application. The loader and libounce perform additional cleanup between NROs, but a living thread can still refer to application code and heap memory. The loader's cleanup and leak checks are evidence that cross-application lifetime management is a real requirement. Loader resource snapshots Application initialization and exit hooks

sections.heading: First hardware acceptance checklist
sections.text: First hardware acceptance checklist - The menu recognizes a native Switch 2 build. - A visible diagnostic frame appears. - HEN transport and initialization results are recorded separately. - Plus exits, and hbmenu becomes usable again. - The application launches again in the same process. - A second, unrelated application can launch afterward. - A missing optional feature produces a clear message and a usable exit path. - The application leaves its own settings intact after an interrupted run. Run the repeated-launch sequence before adding a large dependency. A one-time screenshot proves far less than a clean return followed by another launch.

title: Runtime and ABI
description: Processes, service ownership, loader behavior and protocol boundaries.

sections.heading: Runtime and ABI
sections.text: kaiHEN Runtime Architecture and ABI An application runs inside a loader-managed native game process, while HEN, RO and optional plugins have different lifetimes. Understanding that boundary explains why service ownership, thread shutdown and repeated launches matter as much as the first successful frame.

sections.heading: Launch and execution topology
sections.text: Launch and execution topology The diagram combines the component responsibilities documented by kaiHEN with the loader's application cycle. It is an architectural explanation, not an exploit sequence. kaiHEN project overview Native NRO loader usage HEN starts first and hands plugins their own service sessions. In the inspected bootstrap, a plugin startup failure stops later plugins but does not undo an already-running HEN. Some comments in the plugin header describe older behavior; the bootstrap implementation and current plugin guide establish the sequence used here. Bootstrap launch and plugin readiness Native plugin development guide

sections.heading: Why the first R-held launch differs
sections.text: Why the first R-held launch differs HEN observes native game startup and can substitute the homebrew loader. On the first relevant launch it records the game's signed policy and permits the ordinary game to start; subsequent suitable launches can enter hbmenu. The policy cache affects whether a particular console sees one or two R-held launches during setup. HEN runtime and launch policy For testing, record the host title and whether its policy was already present. Do not classify a normal game launch as an application failure if the environment is still collecting policy. Conversely, the presence of hbmenu is the appropriate point to begin diagnosing an NRO.

sections.heading: The application and process lifetimes
sections.text: The application and process lifetimes The loader starts sdmc:/hbmenu.nro , runs the selected program, and returns to the menu. The process can outlive many individual NROs. Native NRO loader usage Therefore a process-global resource that remains open at application return can affect a later program. This differs from the desktop assumption that process termination will close everything automatically. The loader reserves a 64 MiB loader heap in its current implementation, then uses the remaining region for program staging and the heap override. The number is an implementation detail, not a universal application-memory guarantee. NRO launch cycle and cleanup Avoid a fixed “all RAM is available” assumption. The executable, assets, runtime, loader, renderer and operating-system resource limits all influence useful capacity. Test allocation failure paths rather than sizing an application from the console's advertised hardware memory.

sections.heading: Service overrides and ownership
sections.text: Service overrides and ownership Resource Where it comes from Ownership rule for an application --- --- --- ldr:ro session from kaihenGetRoSession Loader service override Borrowed; do not close the loader's handle HEN session from kaihenOpenHomebrewSession RO creates an independent session Application closes its Service FS or settings clone requested from HEN HEN duplicates the relevant session Close the returned owned handle Process handle requested from HEN Copy for the caller's process Close the copy when finished Plugin session from henOpenPlugin Fresh session factory request Application closes the session These distinctions are explicit in the client interface. A raw numeric handle does not itself encode ownership. kaiHEN client API and handle ownership The FS override is already initialized. libounce deliberately avoids sending SetCurrentProcess again because that would change the identity used by other holders of the shared root. FS initialization and proxy identity Likewise, its SM initialization recognizes the loader's already-initialized override and avoids registering or closing that borrowed session. Service overrides and borrowed SM session For C++, wrap owned handles and services in noncopyable objects with explicit move behavior. Represent borrowed sessions separately. For C, keep ownership flags adjacent to the resource and use a single cleanup path that checks which acquisitions succeeded. Both approaches prevent accidental duplication of cleanup responsibility.

sections.heading: The service-manager proxy
sections.text: The service-manager proxy HEN gives clients independent SM proxy sessions rather than the shared underlying FS-identity session. A malformed or unsupported request can then terminate the offending client connection without taking the shared SM channel away from everyone. The proxy accepts client registration/detachment locally, forwards service lookup, and rejects registration and unregistration of services. Per-client service-manager proxy This does not make every requested service available. A call may fail because of service existence, permissions, request format, firmware behavior, or resource pressure. Log the service name, operation and result before attempting a higher-level recovery.

sections.heading: Protocol layout and negotiation
sections.text: Protocol layout and negotiation The inspected HEN protocol version is 6. HenStatus contains HEN's process ID, protocol version and initialization result. Homebrew command 0 queries status; commands 16–19 return core service or process resources; commands 20–22 enumerate and open published plugins. The protocol defines a 64-byte plugin-name record and a maximum of 16 published plugins. HEN protocol constants and layouts Treat protocol compatibility as feature negotiation. An application using only status should not assume that every future version requires rejection. A feature using commands 20–22 should require their documented availability. Record the protocol value in diagnostics, and distinguish a transport failure from a nonzero initialization result returned in an otherwise successful status reply.

sections.heading: Runtime cleanup
sections.text: Runtime cleanup libounce's exit path closes driver/window hooks, open service guards, the process-shared GSV sync state, and already-exited thread stacks. Its comments explain that those resources would otherwise survive into the next NRO. Application initialization and exit hooks These mechanisms are recovery support. An application should still join its workers, stop audio and network activity, release renderer objects, close files and owned services, then return normally. A live worker executing code from an NRO being unloaded is a correctness failure even if the next menu appears.

sections.heading: ABI design rules
sections.text: ABI design rules Keep application-internal data structures separate from IPC payloads. Use fixed-width integer fields for wire formats, verify structure size and alignment, and avoid C++ object layouts or pointers in messages. The receiver's address space and lifetime differ from the sender's. In particular, an address returned for diagnostic purposes by RO is not automatically a usable application pointer. Prefer library wrappers over direct HIPC construction until a specific missing command requires lower-level work. When direct IPC is necessary, preserve command numbers and payload layouts in a versioned header and validate them with host fixtures plus a minimal console probe.

title: Graphics and UI
description: Vulkan, EGL, OpenGL ES, resolution and presentation.

sections.heading: Graphics and UI
sections.text: kaiHEN Graphics and User Interfaces OunceVK provides the practical native GPU route for this stack. Choose a rendering interface by the application's existing code and feature needs, then validate initialization, presentation and teardown separately.

sections.heading: Rendering paths
sections.text: Rendering paths The driver is derived from Mesa's NVK, with a Switch 2 backend. OpenGL runs through Zink over Vulkan; the driver is linked statically into each program. OunceVK and Mesa overview The SDL2 branch describes the approach used by OunceShell, not a promise about every SDL backend. OunceShell platform source and dependency build Route Suitable starting point Main work to validate --- --- --- CPU console or framebuffer Diagnostics and simple software rendering Buffer conversion cost and presentation SDL2 renderer Existing 2D tools and games Backend selection, textures, fonts, audio and input EGL and GLES Portable mobile-style renderers Context, shader profile and feature queries Direct Vulkan Existing Vulkan engine or explicit GPU control Surface, queues, synchronization and swapchain Switch 1 low-level GPU code Specialized existing renderer Replace or redesign device-specific assumptions

sections.heading: Supported API claims
sections.text: Supported API claims The Switch 2 driver guide advertises Vulkan 1.4, VK_NN_vi_surface on the default NWindow , and EGL-based OpenGL/ES with ES 3.1 stated at the time of writing. These are upstream project claims; this research does not establish Vulkan conformance certification or a tested matrix for every extension. Native graphics interfaces and build guide Query the actual device properties, extensions, queue families, format capabilities and limits used by the application. For GLES, record GL_VERSION , GL_RENDERER , shader-language version and required extensions. A requested context version and a successfully created context are different observations. Mesa's Zink documentation makes clear that exposed functionality depends on both Zink implementation and the underlying Vulkan driver's capabilities. Upstream desktop Zink support therefore does not independently prove an identical Switch 2 feature set. Mesa Zink capabilities documentation

sections.heading: Linking correctly
sections.text: Linking correctly The packaging script builds combined relocatable driver objects and provides libvulkan.a and libEGL.a linker scripts. It also supplies empty compatibility archives for some old Mesa library names to prevent accidental use of the Switch 1 versions. Internal Mesa symbols are localized to reduce application collisions. Static graphics driver packaging Inspect the final link map when porting an existing engine. Two libraries with the same filename can have different platform backends. In particular, a link that succeeds through old portlibs can still select an unsuitable graphics implementation. Because the driver is static, changing the devkit does not update an already-built application. Preserve the driver's revision in application release metadata and rebuild when adopting a graphics fix. The 20261114 GPU-wait change is a concrete example. ounce-devkit 20261114 release

sections.heading: First Vulkan experiment
sections.text: First Vulkan experiment Use the devkit's vulkan-clear example as a reference for the surface and presentation path. It clears swapchain images without shaders, which reduces the number of failure sources in a first GPU experiment. It enables the VI surface platform, creates a surface from nwindowGetDefault , chooses a queue, acquires an image, submits work and presents it. Vulkan clear reference application For a production renderer, extend that baseline with explicit handling for resize or changed surface capabilities, out-of-date swapchains, allocation failures and optional formats. Keep a clear record of which frames are in flight and which synchronization object protects each resource. Do not reuse one acquired image or command buffer before its prior use is complete. A useful debugging progression is: instance, physical device, logical device, surface, swapchain, one clear, repeated presents, one uploaded texture, shaders, then the real scene. Log the first failing call and its return value. Avoid a generalized “GPU failed” message that loses the stage boundary.

sections.heading: First EGL and GLES experiment
sections.text: First EGL and GLES experiment The gles-triangle example creates an EGL display, chooses a GLES 3 configuration, makes a window surface from the default NWindow , creates a context and renders a rotating triangle. It logs the renderer and version strings. GLES triangle reference application For an engine port, add shader compiler and linker logs before loading real content. Check render-target completeness and texture upload formats. A black screen can result from an incorrect viewport, missing vertex binding, invalid shader, wrong framebuffer or no presentation; it does not identify a driver defect by itself. For GLES portability, keep shaders in a deliberate profile and build a small feature test for every nontrivial extension. Avoid silently compiling desktop GLSL through a GLES context.

sections.heading: Resolution and presentation policy
sections.text: Resolution and presentation policy libounce exposes per-mode dimensions and frame-rate policies on its native window API. Window size and frame-rate policies VI2 exposes refresh and capability queries, plus requests for 120 Hz and VRR behavior. The API comments distinguish requests from guaranteed mode changes; system policy and display timings still affect the result. VI2 presentation and display capabilities Treat render resolution, UI scale and output resolution as separate values. A tool can render its 3D scene below output resolution while keeping readable text at an appropriate scale. Recompute viewport and pointer transforms when the drawable extent changes. Record the actual selected extent and refresh rate in performance reports. The hbmenu README describes native-resolution rendering up to 4K at 60 fps. That describes the menu project; it is not a general performance target for arbitrary homebrew. Switch 2 menu usage and rendering

sections.heading: UI architecture
sections.text: UI architecture For file managers and settings tools, use a UI state model independent of rendering. Define actions such as confirm, cancel, next item, pointer click and scroll, then bind controller, touch and pointer input to them. Keep text metrics and focus navigation deterministic. Scale text and hit targets for handheld viewing as well as a television. Preserve focus when a directory refreshes, show progress for long operations, and keep an exit action reachable during recoverable failures. A low frame rate should not cause repeated destructive actions from a held button. Fonts and image decoders can be larger porting dependencies than the initial renderer. OunceShell's build is a useful concrete reference for SDL2_ttf, HarfBuzz, FreeType, image formats and archive libraries. Reuse that dependency knowledge without assuming its entire package set is necessary for a smaller application. OunceShell platform source and dependency build

sections.heading: Graphics diagnostics and shutdown
sections.text: Graphics diagnostics and shutdown OunceVK sends Mesa diagnostics to stderr ; logging options can be set before graphics initialization. Its guide recommends redirecting output to SD and describes a runtime exit hook that closes GPU state. Native graphics interfaces and build guide An application should still wait for or cancel its own work, destroy resources in valid dependency order and release its surface/context. Test a second renderer application immediately after exit. That catches a class of leaked-process-state problems that a first frame cannot reveal.

title: Controllers and pointers
description: PadState, touch and Joy-Con mouse input.

sections.heading: Controllers and pointers
sections.text: kaiHEN Input and Joy-Con Pointers Controller input remains accessible through familiar libnx-style helpers, while Joy-Con mouse input adds a Switch 2-specific path. Applications should combine these into a stable action model and preserve controller navigation when a pointer is absent.

sections.heading: Ordinary controller input
sections.text: Ordinary controller input The PadState API aggregates selected controllers, records current and previous button states, and exposes button-down/button-up edges and stick positions. padInitializeDefault selects the usual first-player and handheld sources. Pad state and controller helpers Use edges for single actions such as opening a menu or confirming a dialog. Use held state for continuous movement. Implement repeat deliberately for list navigation, with an initial delay and a repeat rate, rather than executing an action once per render loop. Map physical buttons into application actions at one boundary. This permits a consistent UI across controller types and leaves room for remapping. Test disconnect and reconnect, handheld-to-docked transitions, multiple connected controllers and a controller becoming inactive while a modal dialog is open.

sections.heading: Touch and conventional mouse
sections.text: Touch and conventional mouse Touch input and ordinary mouse APIs remain distinct from Nmouse. The HID declarations include hidInitializeTouchScreen , touch-state access and the conventional mouse interface. HID touch and conventional input API Design each input path with its own coordinate conversion. A touch event is expressed in a device space; a rendered UI may have letterboxing, scaled content or a viewport offset. Convert to a common logical UI space before hit testing. Keep one source of truth for that transform so drawing and input cannot diverge.

sections.heading: Joy-Con mouse through Nmouse
sections.text: Joy-Con mouse through Nmouse Nmouse supplies samples for Joy-Con and other pointer device types through a dedicated memory registration. Device identifiers are opaque values, not kernel handles or array indices. The inspected API uses a 0xC000 transfer-memory area with page alignment, supports up to two Joy-Con handles per Npad, and retains up to 16 samples per device. Native Nmouse devices and sample memory If the application supplies that memory, it must remain allocated and untouched until successful finalization. A finalization failure means the service may still own it. Treat this as a lifetime rule; freeing a buffer because shutdown “should be done” creates an asynchronous use-after-free risk.

sections.heading: The PadPointer wrapper
sections.text: The PadPointer wrapper PadPointer builds a higher-level pointer from a PadState . Initialize it with the desired logical width and height, call padPointerUpdate after padUpdate , and release it with padPointerExit . It follows the Joy-Con that most recently moved, scrolled or changed a button. PadPointer public declarations The wrapper is an appropriate first implementation for a single visible cursor. Applications needing two independent pointers, raw sample timing or custom merging should inspect the underlying Nmouse API instead. Keep this ordering stable. Mixing rendering and hit testing against different input snapshots can produce clicks on a row that was not visibly selected.

sections.heading: Sample history and frame stalls
sections.text: Sample history and frame stalls The source wrapper accumulates movement from samples newer than its last sampling number, handles device changes and maintains button transitions. Joy-Con pointer aggregation implementation This is useful when the application does not poll at the device's full sample rate. A finite sample ring cannot recover an unlimited stall. Move long operations to workers and keep input polling responsive. For applications that need precise relative movement, test controlled frame stalls and inspect whether the resulting motion meets the product's requirements rather than assuming desktop mouse behavior.

sections.heading: Multiple pointers and focus
sections.text: Multiple pointers and focus Decide whether moving a pointer transfers UI focus immediately or only on click. Decide whether a controller action hides or parks the cursor. Avoid interpreting one physical gesture as two confirmations when conventional mouse, Nmouse and controller paths overlap. For multiplayer tools, associate a pointer with a player or input source explicitly. Do not infer identity from a raw handle's numeric value. On disconnect, release pressed state and preserve the user's current task.

sections.heading: Button mappings and unknown fields
sections.text: Button mappings and unknown fields Nmouse exposes button configuration structures, but the header explicitly leaves some source-button meanings and fields unestablished. Native Nmouse devices and sample memory Keep unknown bits as unknown. Build a diagnostic view that records the observed device type, sample number, movement and recognized buttons, then validate mappings on real controllers. This is especially important for a UI that uses shoulder buttons for pointer clicks while also supporting controller navigation. A mapping that works for one Joy-Con side may be inappropriate for the other.

sections.heading: Input acceptance matrix
sections.text: Input acceptance matrix Scenario Expected behavior --- --- Handheld controller navigation Every primary action reachable Docked controller navigation Focus visible and stable One Joy-Con used as a mouse Cursor and click operate independently of frame rate Left and right Joy-Con movement Chosen ownership policy is predictable Touch on a scaled UI Hit target matches rendered target Reconnect during a held action No stuck button or repeated confirmation Slow directory or network request Input remains usable Pointer initialization unavailable Controller fallback remains functional Store a short interaction trace when investigating failures. “Mouse does not work” is much less useful than a record showing valid samples but a bad viewport transform, or no handles despite successful initialization.

title: Files, network and media
description: Storage, sockets, audio and hardware video decoding.

sections.heading: Files, network and media
sections.text: kaiHEN Files Networking Audio and Video Most useful applications combine file access with one or more asynchronous systems. Keep storage, networking, audio and decoding behind separate interfaces so each can be diagnosed and shut down independently.

sections.heading: Filesystem access
sections.text: Filesystem access libounce supplies the familiar FS service and newlib device layer. Under kaiHEN, the initialized FS proxy override has special identity semantics, so use the library initialization path rather than reinitializing a borrowed root manually. FS initialization and proxy identity The filesystem device implementation adapts operations into standard file APIs. Standard filesystem device adapter Use romfs:/ for read-only packaged data after mounting RomFS, and an application-specific sdmc:/switch/<app / directory for state. These names are mount conventions. They do not impose access restrictions on code that has broader service access. RomFS mount API For settings, use a versioned file format and bounds-checked parsing. Write a new version to a temporary file, flush and close it, then replace the old file through a carefully checked sequence. Validate replacement and durability behavior on the actual filesystem; a rename by itself is not a proof of crash-safe persistence. Keep logs, caches, user documents and migration backups in distinguishable locations. Limit cleanup routines to their own generated paths. A file browser should normalize paths and distinguish navigation from an operation's intended destination before beginning a copy or delete.

sections.heading: Storage test cases
sections.text: Storage test cases Test no writable destination, full storage, an interrupted write, a corrupt configuration, an unexpected filename, a directory where a file is expected, and a large asset that cannot fit in memory. For copy operations, compare byte counts and a hash when correctness matters. Do not label a transfer complete merely because a socket closed or a progress bar reached its predicted total. For game-related tools, keep save handling and raw storage operations separate from ordinary application files. This pack does not establish that any particular save operation is safe for every title. A general-purpose utility should expose a narrow task rather than enabling raw system writes as part of routine startup.

sections.heading: Network initialization
sections.text: Network initialization The runtime exposes socketInitializeDefault and socketExit , while NIFM provides network-service functionality. Socket runtime initialization Network interface service API A project using these APIs still needs to verify the requested services under its runtime and host-title combination. Design network operations with explicit timeouts, cancellation and bounded buffers. Distinguish name-resolution errors, connection failures, protocol errors and server-side rejection. Network loss should leave local documents and settings consistent. Do not run a blocking connect, receive or TLS handshake on the UI thread. Give each request an ownership model: which thread may cancel it, which object receives completion, and whether the result can arrive after the screen has changed. This prevents a stale completion callback from accessing freed application state.

sections.heading: Development file transfer
sections.text: Development file transfer OunceShell bundles an FTP server and a file manager. Its Switch 2 port adapts networking and filesystem functions through a platform layer. OunceShell project and upstream context Network compatibility layer It is a practical way to copy application builds and retrieve logs when the environment is already running. For a development loop, upload to a temporary filename, verify the transfer, then make the final name visible. Keep the previous known-good NRO until the new build has launched and exited. Transfer transport and application correctness are separate checks. Use a network you control for development services. If the application exposes a listener, define its bind address, authentication and permitted operations explicitly. Avoid a general remote command channel when the product only needs a fixed set of file or diagnostic requests.

sections.heading: HTTP and TLS dependencies
sections.text: HTTP and TLS dependencies An HTTP client library compiling from portlibs does not prove certificate validation, clock handling, entropy or TLS backends work on the target. For a networked product, test an expected valid certificate, an expired certificate, a hostname mismatch and a disconnected network. Preserve verification errors rather than disabling checks to make a request succeed. The exact HTTPS library and certificate-store solution are application choices requiring their own validation. The core kaiHEN sources inspected here do not define a universal web-client configuration. A local-only application can avoid that dependency entirely.

sections.heading: Audio path
sections.text: Audio path The Switch 2-specific aud:u root supplies AudioOut and AudioRenderer managers. libounce routes its audout and audren initialization through that root for native Switch 2 builds, preserving higher-level API names while changing service acquisition. Native audio manager root AudioOut native service selection AudioRenderer native service selection For a new application, prove one short PCM output before adding decoding, mixing, effects or streaming. Check returned sample rate, channel layout and format rather than assuming the requested values were selected. Retain buffers until the service reports that they are no longer in use. For streaming audio, use a bounded ring buffer and measure underruns. Separate decoding from the real-time consumption path. Avoid allocation, filesystem scans or network waits in an audio callback. During shutdown, stop consumption before freeing buffers and join any thread that can still submit audio. OunceShell includes a Vita audio compatibility layer implemented with SDL audio. It is a useful example of adapting an existing application-level API instead of porting the original device code directly. SDL audio compatibility layer

sections.heading: Hardware video decoding
sections.text: Hardware video decoding libounce exposes a VideoDecoder abstraction over native services. It owns service sessions, work memory and output images, and returns NV12 frames with explicit release. The declared aggregate pixel-rate limit is 248832000 pixels per second, with a per-decoder frame-rate ceiling of 60. AV1 uses block-linear output in the documented path. High-level hardware video decoder API The lower-level codec enum includes H.264, VP9, AV1 and VP8; it does not establish support for every profile or an undeclared codec. Decoder codecs and low-level image API A demuxer, container parser, network transport, A/V clock and presentation pipeline remain application responsibilities. A 4K decoder is a substantial memory consumer: the header's documented working-memory examples are roughly 272 MiB for pitch-linear and 308 MiB for block-linear, plus output images. These are examples tied to the current implementation, not a universal allocation formula. High-level hardware video decoder API Start media experiments with a small, known encoded sample, then add demuxing and sustained playback. Record codec, profile, dimensions, frame rate, timestamps, output layout and decoder result. A single decoded frame does not prove seeking, end-of-stream handling or long playback.

sections.heading: Backpressure and synchronization
sections.text: Backpressure and synchronization If every output image is held, a decoder cannot continue producing frames. Release frames promptly after consumption, and synchronize image access before returning them. The native graphics/video interface exposes producer and consumer synchronization concepts; ignoring those lifetimes can produce corruption that resembles a decoder failure. Graphics image and synchronization API Decoder synchronization and lifetime implementation For an initial player, a CPU copy into a conventional texture may simplify validation at the cost of bandwidth. A zero-copy path needs verified layout compatibility, synchronization and ownership across decoding and rendering. Do not advertise it based only on the presence of image IDs or GPU addresses.

sections.heading: Integrated shutdown order
sections.text: Integrated shutdown order For a streaming player: stop network input, stop creating new decode work, drain or cancel the pipeline, release outstanding video frames, stop audio consumption, join workers, close decoder and graphics resources, then close sockets and files. The precise sequence depends on which subsystem owns each buffer. Write that ownership down before implementing recovery from a disconnect.

title: JIT and language runtimes
description: Code publication, emulation, memory and cache synchronization.

sections.heading: JIT and language runtimes
sections.text: kaiHEN JIT Emulation and Language Runtimes kaiHEN exposes a JIT backend that lets applications retain the familiar libnx Jit interface while RO performs privileged mapping and publication work. This is useful for dynamic recompilers, but it introduces staging, synchronization and lifetime costs that must be designed into the runtime.

sections.heading: Public interface and provider
sections.text: Public interface and provider Applications use jitCreate , jitGetRwAddr , jitGetRxAddr , transition calls and jitClose . Linking -lkaihen selects the provider object installed by the devkit. That object arrangement matters because the library hooks are weak references and can otherwise be omitted by ordinary archive extraction. JIT backend development guide JIT provider and plugin library build Test the final link, not just the presence of a header. Record an actual successful JIT creation in diagnostics, and retain an interpreter or non-JIT path when the application architecture permits it.

sections.heading: Mapping and publication model
sections.text: Mapping and publication model The RW address returned to the application is staging memory, not a directly coherent physical alias of executable memory. The RX address remains mapped across logical writable/executable transitions. Full publication copies staging contents through RO; sparse publication can send selected ranges. JIT backend development guide This means a port that assumes “writing the RW alias immediately changes code visible at RX” needs modification. The writable-to-executable transition is a publication operation and can fail. Never call newly generated code after a failed publication simply because the pointer is non-null.

sections.heading: Memory and mapping costs
sections.text: Memory and mapping costs libounce rounds a requested JIT allocation to pages, reserves executable address space and, for the alias backend, allocates a separate staging region in addition to backing memory. JIT allocation and transition implementation An approximate application budget is therefore: That is a planning model, not a measured heap total. A 64 MiB code cache can require approximately another 64 MiB of staging before allocator overhead. Budget the emulator's RAM, textures, audio buffers and recompilation metadata separately. RO's current helper has 512 JIT-record slots per initialized client session. This is a bookkeeping ceiling, not a guarantee that the kernel or available memory permits 512 live allocations of any size. RO client and JIT bookkeeping limits Prefer a measured number of larger arenas when the emitter can manage them safely. Thousands of tiny mappings may hit record limits long before raw memory is exhausted. Conversely, publishing an entire oversized arena for a tiny patch can waste IPC and copy bandwidth.

sections.heading: Sparse publication
sections.text: Sparse publication kaihenJitPublishRanges accepts byte ranges within staging. Its implementation validates ranges, combines eligible adjacent regions and packages publication data. JIT provider and sparse publication The RO side validates the payload and writes through the retained mapping. RO command validation and JIT publication For a dynamic recompiler, collect dirty code intervals during one compilation batch, merge overlapping or adjacent intervals in a well-defined way, then publish once per safe batch. Measure copied bytes, request count and publish latency. Do not assume the helper's coalescing alone eliminates all emitter-side overhead.

sections.heading: Multi-threaded execution
sections.text: Multi-threaded execution Publication invalidates the calling thread's instruction range. Other threads entering new code need their own synchronization and instruction-cache handling. Code must not be modified while another thread executes it, and readers must stop before a mapping is closed. JIT backend development guide A straightforward design uses immutable code blocks: generate a new block, publish it, atomically make it reachable through a dispatch structure, then retire the old block only after all readers have left. This is an engineering pattern, not a facility automatically provided by kaiHEN. For an initial port, keep emission and execution on one thread until the basic correctness path works. Add concurrent compilation only after defining publication barriers, entry-point visibility and reclamation.

sections.heading: Cleanup and failed unmapping
sections.text: Cleanup and failed unmapping The RO implementation tracks mapping ownership and retains records when cleanup cannot complete. RO mapping and cleanup implementation The loader sends the release-all-JIT command when an NRO returns before reusing program memory. NRO launch cycle and cleanup An emulator should still close its own JIT objects and report cleanup failures. Reusing code-cache memory after a failed unmap can invalidate the ownership assumptions that made earlier mappings safe. A teardown failure should stop the normal restart path until the environment has been reconciled.

sections.heading: Emulator porting sequence
sections.text: Emulator porting sequence 1. Build the portable core in interpreter mode and validate input/output on the host. 2. Run a small native frontend with file loading and a known legal test program. 3. Verify graphics and audio independently. 4. Add one JIT arena and a minimal generated function. 5. Compare interpreter and recompiler outputs on deterministic fixtures. 6. Add invalidation and self-modifying-code cases relevant to the emulated system. 7. Test repeated startup, cache reset and exit. 8. Optimize only after recording publication and execution costs. The exact tests depend on the guest system. A screenshot or a speed increase is not enough to establish instruction correctness, exception behavior or memory-ordering correctness.

sections.heading: Language choices
sections.text: Language choices C and C++ are the most directly demonstrated application languages in the devkit examples. Rust is present in OunceVK's build, including a custom target and standard-library build machinery, but that does not by itself establish a polished general Rust application SDK for kaiHEN. Driver Rust target definition For Rust, begin with a small C ABI bridge to a validated libounce application and prove allocation, panic behavior, threads and NRO startup before importing a large framework. Pin target and linker choices. Existing Switch 1 Rust guides need a separate review for platform-specific service and graphics assumptions. Lua or another interpreter can be embedded as portable C code, subject to build and runtime validation. Do not assume a language's upstream JIT supports this environment simply because it emits AArch64. It may depend on mmap , protection changes, signal handling or instruction-cache behavior that need an explicit adaptation. For a large engine, expose a narrow native host API to scripts: input actions, assets, timing, rendering commands and application state. This keeps script portability separate from system-service access and makes deterministic host tests possible.

title: Plugins and IPC
description: Resident NSOs, service discovery and command design.

sections.heading: Plugins and IPC
sections.text: kaiHEN Plugins IPC and Services Native plugins are separate resident processes. Use one when work must continue outside an individual NRO, when several applications need a shared service, or when an operation has a clearly defined process boundary. Ordinary application features are easier to develop and recover when they remain in the application.

sections.heading: Plugin lifecycle
sections.text: Plugin lifecycle The bootstrap scans .nso files under /kaihen/plugins . A plugin receives its own SM-proxy session and FS-root clone through a temporary startup handoff. pluginRuntimeInitialize installs the necessary overrides. A plugin that uses files explicitly initializes and exits FS. Plugin runtime handoff and teardown The plugin signals a ready event after completing its own initialization. The bootstrap currently waits up to five seconds. A timed-out plugin may keep running while remaining absent from HEN's published service list; /kaihen/plugin-status.txt records startup outcomes. Native plugin development guide Readiness must mean that the advertised commands are usable. A process existing is not the same as a service being ready. Allocate mandatory resources and start the service loop before signaling the ready event.

sections.heading: Build model
sections.text: Build model The reference plugin uses AppletType_None , supplies its own small heap, replaces application initialization hooks, links -lkaihen_plugin -lounce_core , and converts an ELF into an NSO. Native plugin ELF and NSO build Resident echo plugin example The -lounce_core choice keeps the small plugin on newlib's allocator rather than the normal application mimalloc arrangement. Do not copy a large application's heap assumptions into a resident process. Start with a fixed, measured workload and expose memory use in diagnostics.

sections.heading: Publishing an IPC service
sections.text: Publishing an IPC service pluginRuntimeInitialize alone does not publish a service. The opt-in function pluginRuntimeInitializeWithService returns the ready event and a borrowed control-session handle. pluginServiceStart can then serve scalar commands. The simple helper supports up to 64 request bytes and 64 reply bytes, with a maximum of 16 client sessions. Native plugin public interface HEN publishes the plugin under its filename without .nso . Each client opening it receives a fresh session. Current plugin enumeration is not a list of every running plugin; it is a list of those that published IPC and remain eligible for listing. HEN command and plugin discovery server For larger data, transferred handles, domains or mapped buffers, use a deliberately designed custom HIPC/CMIF server rather than forcing a bulk transfer through a scalar command structure. The server-side helper code is the appropriate starting point for understanding parsing and reply construction. Server-side CMIF helpers

sections.heading: Client flow
sections.text: Client flow An application obtains RO's borrowed session, opens an owned HEN session, queries status, enumerates names and opens the desired plugin. The devkit's echo client demonstrates a simple scalar request and writes the result to SD. Plugin discovery and scalar client example Use a version-query command in the plugin's own protocol. HEN protocol version 6 establishes the discovery mechanism, but it does not describe each plugin's application-specific commands. Two plugins with the same filename can still expose incompatible payloads. If a plugin disappears, close the failed client session and present an unavailable state. A cached name or process ID is not a durable authority across restarts. Do not automatically repeat a mutating request whose completion is uncertain after a timeout; design request IDs and status queries when retry safety matters.

sections.heading: Command design
sections.text: Command design A small service protocol should define: Element Required decision --- --- Version Major/minor policy and supported features Request identity Command ID, optional sequence and retry semantics Payload Fixed-width fields, size and permitted ranges Reply Transport result, operation result and output size Lifetime Which side owns buffers, handles and sessions Cancellation Whether a pending operation can be stopped Limits Maximum work, queue depth and concurrent clients CMIF can pad scalar input to whole words. Validate the minimum known payload and read only its declared fields, rather than assuming the callback's byte count equals the logical struct size. Scalar plugin service implementation Avoid exposing pointers, arbitrary paths or a generic system-call proxy when a bounded operation will serve the product. A file-index service, for example, can accept a validated directory identifier and return a bounded batch of entries. That is easier to test and recover than a fully general remote filesystem interface.

sections.heading: Threading and slow work
sections.text: Threading and slow work The helper separates the control thread answering HEN's fresh-session requests from the worker thread handling client commands. That protects HEN from a slow plugin callback. Scalar plugin service implementation It does not mean all client commands run in parallel. For long tasks, accept a job and return a job ID promptly. Provide status, result and cancellation commands with bounded replies. Keep service control responsive while file scans, transfers or computations run elsewhere. Define queue saturation behavior; an unbounded queue turns a temporary slow client into a resident memory problem.

sections.heading: Shutdown and error handling
sections.text: Shutdown and error handling Stop the service before calling pluginRuntimeExit . The runtime owns its startup handles; the borrowed control session should not be closed separately by client code. Native plugin public interface Close every plugin-owned resource on each initialization failure path. If the service cannot start, report a specific result and avoid signaling ready. If a worker fails after publication, expose the failed state and release clients in a controlled way. A plugin persists beyond an application, so include a way to inspect its state without running its full workload. Useful fields include protocol version, uptime, active sessions, queued jobs, memory counters and last operation result. Keep the diagnostic interface read-only.

sections.heading: Validation plan
sections.text: Validation plan Test successful startup, missing file, initialization failure, readiness timeout, malformed scalar input, unknown command, maximum sessions, client disconnect during work, service shutdown and plugin process exit. Add a deliberately slow command to confirm that HEN's discovery remains responsive. The development-kit echo example is particularly useful because it includes ordinary request handling, an exit event and a deliberately slow command. Study those mechanics before replacing them with a real workload. Resident echo plugin example Finally, test ordinary NRO launch and return while the plugin is active. The relevant acceptance criterion is coexistence across several application cycles, not simply that the plugin process starts.

title: Port an existing app
description: Dependencies, framework choices and concrete porting examples.

sections.heading: Port an existing app
sections.text: kaiHEN Porting Frameworks and Case Studies Porting effort is determined by the lowest-level assumptions in an application. Inventory those assumptions before selecting a renderer or importing an entire dependency graph.

sections.heading: Porting categories
sections.text: Porting categories Existing project Likely reusable parts Main adaptation work --- --- --- Portable C or C++ library Algorithms and ordinary data handling Cross-build, allocation and filesystem behavior libnx utility Application logic and many service wrappers Switch 2 rules, service access and lifecycle SDL2 application UI/game logic, input abstraction and assets Library selection, backend and device testing OpenGL ES application Most renderer structure EGL setup, shader profile and extensions Vulkan application Renderer organization and shaders VI surface, limits, synchronization and presentation Low-level Switch 1 renderer Higher-level scene or UI logic Device interfaces, memory layout and shader backend Dynamic recompiler Guest-system logic and some emitter code JIT publication, cache coordination and ownership Desktop engine Portable subsystems Platform layer, build graph and unsupported OS features This is an engineering estimate. It is not a compatibility matrix. The devkit states that Switch portlibs depending only on the C library and libnx, such as SDL2, can be reused. Low-level backend assumptions still require testing in the application that links them. Development kit installation and usage

sections.heading: Dependency inventory
sections.text: Dependency inventory For every dependency, record its purpose, target platform, license identifier, whether it is static, whether it uses OS services, and whether it assumes a desktop process model. Prioritize libraries that touch graphics, threads, memory protection, sockets, audio and filesystem paths. Common hidden assumptions include dynamic library loading, Unix signals, subprocesses, writable executable memory, desktop font directories, /tmp , unrestricted thread creation and a process exit that closes all resources. Replacing a compiler flag cannot resolve these architectural dependencies.

sections.heading: A staged porting workflow
sections.text: A staged porting workflow 1. Preserve a working host build and deterministic fixtures. 2. Build a native empty application with the pinned devkit. 3. Add the portable core without graphics or networking. 4. Add asset access and validate formats. 5. Add input and one rendering frame. 6. Add audio and background work. 7. Run representative workloads. 8. Test repeated launch, failure and exit. 9. Optimize measured bottlenecks. Keep each milestone small enough that a failing console log identifies a subsystem. A large first merge with a renderer, decoder, JIT and UI framework gives almost no diagnostic leverage when startup fails.

sections.heading: Case study OunceShell
sections.text: Case study OunceShell OunceShell adapts VitaShell into a Switch 2 file manager with browsing, editors, media functions and FTP. Its top-level README includes inherited Vita documentation, so platform-specific behavior should be checked in the switch2 sources rather than inferred from every upstream paragraph. OunceShell project and upstream context Its build selects portable VitaShell sources and a replacement platform layer. Functions for IO, networking, controller input, time, kernel-style utilities, text entry and rendering are adapted under switch2/src . OunceShell platform source and dependency build The renderer compatibility layer maps the old application's drawing concepts onto SDL, while the audio adapter uses SDL audio. SDL rendering compatibility layer SDL audio compatibility layer Initialization sets up Switch 2 resources and installs defaults beneath sdmc:/switch/ounceshell/ ; unsupported Vita system features are deliberately left out. OunceShell native initialization Deliberately unsupported inherited functions The general lesson is to preserve a mature application's internal contracts and replace the narrow platform boundary. This can be more tractable than rewriting the UI, file model and document operations at once. It also makes unsupported features visible instead of leaving them as nonfunctional menu items. This case study does not mean every Vita application can use the same compatibility layer unchanged. The relevant artifact is the set of platform abstractions and their assumptions.

sections.heading: Case study hbmenu
sections.text: Case study hbmenu The Switch 2 hbmenu replaces CPU rendering with Vulkan and adds native-resolution rendering and vector assets. Its source separates rendering, Vulkan graphics and performance instrumentation. Menu render adapter Menu Vulkan renderer Menu performance instrumentation For a UI port, this suggests a practical split: keep application navigation and data handling, replace the render backend, then address resolution, fonts and timing explicitly. Treat a high-resolution icon or framebuffer as part of a whole scaling policy rather than an isolated cosmetic upgrade. The project also recognizes platform metadata to warn about non-native programs. A distributor can reduce confusion further by using explicit Switch 2 artifact names and metadata in its own release process. Menu launch and platform identification

sections.heading: Engine selection
sections.text: Engine selection For a small new application, SDL2 or a small EGL/GLES renderer has a lower integration surface than a full desktop engine. For an existing Vulkan codebase, retaining Vulkan may save more work than translating the renderer. Select based on the actual project rather than a universal preference. This research does not establish turnkey kaiHEN exports for Unity, Unreal, Godot, Electron, Python or every Rust framework. Official console SDK support and an open homebrew build target are different integration paths. A framework candidate should first build a minimal application through this stack, then prove its renderer, input, audio, threads and shutdown. For a large C++ engine, maintain a platform/switch2 layer with explicit capabilities. Disable unavailable subsystems through configuration rather than scattered edits. Keep the portable engine buildable on the host so unit tests and content tools remain usable.

sections.heading: Community project directory
sections.text: Community project directory The ouncebrew list links tools, games, streaming applications, emulators and plugins. Examples include Checkpoint, NXGallery, Sonic 3 AIR, Sonic Robo Blast 2, Moonlight, RetroArch, mGBA and an FTP plugin. Community application and plugin directory Use those entries to find candidate implementations of a subsystem. Before borrowing an approach, inspect the actual repository, its target branch, build instructions and dependency pins. A listing says little about whether its binary was rebuilt for the current driver or tested with the firmware available to you. Avoid treating a similarly named project, a screenshot or a download label as proof of a working build. For every adopted component, preserve the exact source revision and its tested environment.

sections.heading: Port completion criteria
sections.text: Port completion criteria A useful port should preserve the original application's important behavior, integrate platform input and storage conventions, recover from unavailable services, return cleanly, and document remaining limitations. Performance should be measured on representative workloads rather than an empty menu. Compare host and console outputs for parsers, save formats, game simulation or media metadata where deterministic comparison is possible. For rendering and interaction, use a scenario list and recorded hardware observations. Compilation is one milestone; feature parity and reliability require additional evidence.

title: Debugging and testing
description: Failure diagnosis, profiling and meaningful verification.

sections.heading: Debugging and testing
sections.text: kaiHEN Debugging Performance and Testing Diagnose a failure at the narrowest boundary where it is observable. Separate environment acquisition, loader behavior, runtime initialization, application logic and rendering so that each result supports a specific conclusion.

sections.heading: Evidence ladder
sections.text: Evidence ladder Observation What it establishes What it leaves open --- --- --- Headers and source exist An interface is implemented or declared Build and hardware behavior Host fixture passes Tested logic works in that fixture Kernel, devices and console services Cross-compilation succeeds Chosen sources and link inputs form an artifact Startup and runtime compatibility NRO launches Entry and initial runtime path execute All features and cleanup First visible frame One graphics path presents Sustained use and synchronization Exit and relaunch work A specific lifecycle sequence succeeds Other workloads and failure paths Sustained scenario passes Recorded behavior in one environment Universal compatibility Use these levels in release notes and bug reports. This prevents a host test, a build or a screenshot from becoming a broader claim than its evidence supports.

sections.heading: Log design
sections.text: Log design Write a startup record containing application commit, devkit version, driver/library pins, runtime release, protocol, host title, configured features and actual display properties. Add the exact firmware from a trusted system query or a recorded system-settings observation; do not infer it solely from compatibility markers. libounce's hosversionGet masks environment marker bits and can use a 20.0.0 default in native Switch 2 startup. Its comments also describe hbloader passing a compatibility version. Therefore a bare hosversionGet value is not sufficient to prove the console's installed firmware in every launch path. Firmware compatibility markers and defaults For each subsystem, log start, selected configuration, result and cleanup. Use monotonic timestamps and one operation identifier. Preserve the first failure before later cleanup errors overwrite it.

sections.heading: Result handling
sections.text: Result handling Record raw Result values in hexadecimal along with the operation name. Distinguish IPC transport success from a status structure's reported initialization result. For POSIX-style APIs, capture errno immediately after the failing call before another library call changes it. Treat timeout as its own state. A timeout does not prove that a remote mutation did not occur. For file transfer or service operations that can modify data, include an operation identifier and a read-back method before adding automatic retry.

sections.heading: Symptom map
sections.text: Symptom map Symptom First boundary to inspect Useful next evidence --- --- --- Game opens instead of hbmenu HEN policy/arming stage Host title, prior policy and launch sequence Menu warns about the program NRO platform metadata Clean rebuild and selected runtime Immediate application exit Initialization stages First logged call and result Black screen Render and presentation stages Device strings, surface extent, shader logs Sound fails to initialize Audio service acquisition aud:u path and result Joy-Con mouse absent Nmouse setup and device discovery Init result, handles and sample count JIT unavailable Provider linking and runtime path Final link command and jitCreate result Second application fails Resource lifetime Thread, service and GPU cleanup records Intermittent device loss GPU wait/synchronization and driver version OunceVK revision and reduced reproduction

sections.heading: Host tests in the upstream sources
sections.text: Host tests in the upstream sources The HEN test script compiles fixtures for code-mount requests and SM decoding. The RO script tests wire decoding, image layout, client sessions and mapping against mock backends. Their configured flags include address and undefined-behavior sanitizers, while disabling alignment checks for the wire parser's intentionally unaligned fields. HEN host test commands RO host test commands Mocked mapping tests cannot prove console kernel mappings or actual service registration. The RO README makes that limitation explicit. RO implementation and test scope During this research, the default host invocation failed to compile under the installed Apple Clang because of constexpr diagnostics in the HIPC headers. Retrying with CXX='clang++ -Wno-invalid-constexpr' compiled the first fixtures, but both suites stopped with Trace/BPT trap and exit 133. The trap's cause was not established. These local suites did not pass; their logs are retained in research/validation/ . This is a bounded result for this host and invocation, not proof that the upstream tests fail on their intended environment. No source files were changed to make them pass. A clean Linux/GNU toolchain run is a sensible next verification step, followed by hardware tests where relevant.

sections.heading: Application tests
sections.text: Application tests Use host tests for meaningful portable behavior: configuration migration, path validation, binary parsing, transfer state machines, queue limits and deterministic simulation. Avoid tests that merely duplicate a function's implementation line for line. On hardware, test initialize/fail/unwind, launch/exit/relaunch, an unrelated application after exit, input reconnect, missing files, full storage, network disconnect, renderer initialization failure and sustained workload. If a test changes storage, use disposable application-owned fixtures. Preserve expected and observed outcomes. “Tested on Switch 2” is not a reproducible test record without firmware, runtime, devkit, workload and artifact hash.

sections.heading: Timing and CPU performance
sections.text: Timing and CPU performance libounce's native tick helpers use a 31.25 MHz counter model, equivalent to 32 ns per tick, and expose the counter-frequency register. Tick frequency and time conversion Do not reuse an old Switch 1 hard-coded conversion in an engine profiler. Record distributions instead of only average FPS. Useful metrics include median frame time, slow-frame percentiles, maximum stall, startup time, asset-load duration and input-to-action delay. Measure UI idle and active workloads separately. Instrument CPU update, rendering preparation, GPU wait, presentation and background IO.

sections.heading: Memory performance
sections.text: Memory performance Normal libounce applications use mimalloc. Its heapGetTotalSize and heapGetFreeSize helpers describe that allocator's heap, while newlib's mallinfo and sbrk do not describe the same state. The free-size helper is a lower bound that excludes free space within partly used allocator pages. Allocator-aware heap measurements Track allocation peaks and subsystem budgets: assets, render targets, compressed data, decoded media, JIT staging and worker queues. A decreasing “free” counter is a symptom to investigate, not automatically a leak. Compare equivalent checkpoints after repeated workloads and teardown.

sections.heading: GPU and lifecycle diagnostics
sections.text: GPU and lifecycle diagnostics hbmenu includes an optional performance overlay and platform timing instrumentation. Menu performance instrumentation OunceVK's native backend has completion and progress code that distinguishes pending work from completed work; its recent wait fix makes exact driver identity important when reporting device loss. Native GPU completion waits Native GPU progress ownership The loader also snapshots resources and reports remaining threads, handles, memory and map changes after an NRO. Its cleanup code should be read before assuming every reported difference is harmless. Loader resource snapshots NRO launch cycle and cleanup Reduce failures to the smallest workload that preserves the symptom. A useful report contains a minimal source commit, build inputs, exact steps, first failing call, full relevant log, frequency and a comparison against a known-good version. Include hardware captures only when they add information the logs cannot express.

title: Package and release
description: Metadata, artifacts, dependency licenses and release gates.

sections.heading: Package and release
sections.text: kaiHEN Packaging Distribution and Development Roadmap Ship an application as a traceable build with clear requirements and a tested lifecycle. A good release tells another developer exactly what was built, how it was validated and which features remain conditional.

sections.heading: Application package layout
sections.text: Application package layout A conventional application package can contain: This is a suggested distribution convention. Keep mutable settings and downloaded content outside the archive's overwrite-sensitive files. Include required external assets only when their distribution is authorized; otherwise explain how the user supplies them. For the environment itself, the verified kaiHEN archive contains bootstrap.bin , hbmenu.nro , ro/main , hen/main , game/main , programs/ounceshell.nro and license files. These are different artifacts from an application's own .nro . kaiHEN 20261114c release

sections.heading: Metadata and artifact identity
sections.text: Metadata and artifact identity Use an unambiguous artifact name such as myapp-switch2-v0.1.0.nro . Populate application title, author and version through NACP generation, and retain a recognizable icon. The reference Makefile documents those fields and NRO asset options. GLES example NRO build pipeline Generate SHA-256 hashes for the distributable and preserve its unstripped ELF and linker map privately or as developer artifacts. Record source commits for the application and the static runtime/driver dependencies. Use the downloadable build record template and hardware test record to preserve the exact environment and results. Separate release version from tested environment. An application version may be unchanged while a rebuild adopts a new OunceVK. Indicate that dependency change explicitly, because the binary's graphics behavior can change even when application source does not.

sections.heading: Minimum release notes
sections.text: Minimum release notes Field Useful content --- --- Purpose What the application does and its primary workflow Requirements Native Switch 2 environment, runtime/devkit baseline, required services Installation Exact SD directory and external assets Controls Confirm, cancel, exit and optional pointer/touch actions Data Where settings, logs and user content are stored Validation Firmware, host title, artifact hash and scenarios tested Limitations Unsupported functions and recoverable failure behavior Changes Application and dependency changes Sources Repository and exact source revision Avoid “works on all Switch 2 consoles” unless the evidence actually supports that scope. A correct narrower statement is more useful to a developer diagnosing a mismatch.
