sections.text: Dependency licenses The inspected projects declare different licenses: Component Declared license or license family --- --- kaiHEN core GPL-2.0-only with the repository's named exemption libkaihen ISC libounce and inherited libnx code ISC; bundled mimalloc is MIT ounce-devkit packaging MIT hbloader and hbmenu ISC, with separately licensed bundled dependencies OunceShell GPL-3.0-or-later, with separately licensed dependencies OunceVK/Mesa Per-file and bundled license texts Use the exact license files for the revisions you ship; the runtime release's licenses/ directory is a useful inventory example. This table records project declarations and does not resolve a particular product's redistribution obligations. kaiHEN core license libkaihen license libounce inherited runtime license Devkit packaging license Loader license Menu license OunceShell and VitaShell license Mesa licensing reference For a release pipeline, inventory what actually links into the binary rather than relying on only the top-level repository license. Preserve notices and review third-party assets, fonts and codecs alongside code dependencies.

sections.heading: Continuous integration
sections.text: Continuous integration A practical CI pipeline builds portable host targets, runs meaningful host tests, cross-compiles the native application, stores logs and symbols, and assembles a versioned artifact with hashes. Hardware acceptance remains a separate recorded step unless a reliable device test rig exists. Pin toolchain and source inputs. Keep the host test build separate from the cross build so a host library cannot accidentally satisfy a target dependency. Fail the release when required assets are missing, the expected NRO is absent or a hash manifest does not match the artifact being uploaded. If CI cannot run the application, label that limitation directly. “CI passed” then means the configured checks passed, not that gameplay, audio or GPU execution succeeded.

sections.heading: Suggested milestone roadmap
sections.text: Suggested milestone roadmap Milestone Deliverable Acceptance gate --- --- --- 0 Platform baseline Recorded console/runtime/toolchain combination Environment reproducible and source pins saved 1 Native diagnostic Small NRO with status and exit Launch, exit and relaunch on hardware 2 Portable core Main algorithms and data model Host fixtures and known data agree 3 Interaction and assets UI/input with real content Controller fallback and file errors handled 4 Rendering and sound Representative frame and audio Sustained use without corruption or underruns 5 Optional services Network, decoder, JIT or plugin Independent feature probes and cleanup pass 6 Reliability Recovery paths and resource tracking Repeated mixed-application cycles pass 7 Release candidate Package, manifest and notes Artifact identity and hardware matrix reviewed These are suggested gates, not estimated completion dates. A small utility may skip several optional systems; an emulator or streaming client will spend more time on their interactions.

sections.heading: Maintaining compatibility
sections.text: Maintaining compatibility When adopting a new runtime or devkit, rebuild from clean directories, compare link maps, run the minimal diagnostic, then repeat representative workloads and lifecycle tests. Record regressions against the last known-good artifact. Track upstream changes by subsystem. A graphics fix suggests rendering and presentation tests; a loader cleanup change suggests repeated-launch tests; a plugin protocol change suggests discovery and payload tests. This is more efficient than retesting every scenario for every documentation edit, while still responding to consequential code changes.

sections.heading: Release-readiness decision
sections.text: Release-readiness decision Publish when the application's main workflow, failure behavior and exit path have been observed on the stated environment, and the package can be reproduced from its inputs. Keep experiments available as clearly labeled developer builds when those gates remain open. The label should tell users what evidence exists, not hide uncertainty behind a generic beta designation.

sections.heading: Local validation outcome
sections.text: Local validation outcome The HEN and RO host suites were attempted using the inspected libounce headers. The default Apple Clang invocation failed on HIPC constexpr diagnostics. A second invocation suppressing that diagnostic compiled the first fixture in each suite, but execution stopped with Trace/BPT trap and exit code 133. The cause remains unresolved. The suites did not pass on this host. Exact compiler identity, commands and captured output are retained under validation/ . No devkit was installed, no native application was cross-compiled, and no console operation, firmware change, save modification or hardware test was performed. The illustrative application is source material for a future build, not a tested release. This publication preserves the original research scope; site behavior is verified separately from console behavior.

title: Quickstart
description: The shortest path from a clean build to your first native NRO.

sections.heading: Quickstart
sections.text: Quickstart Build a small native Switch 2 application before adding an engine or a resident plugin. This path gets the toolchain, graphics, controller input and normal exit onto one reproducible baseline.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.text: Before you begin You need a development computer, devkitPro's Switch toolchain, the ounce-devkit overlay, and a supported console environment for running the resulting NRO. Building on your computer does not require a live console. The research baseline is ounce-devkit 20261114 and kaiHEN 20261114c . Treat these as a pinned reference rather than a claim about every later release. Read Platform overview for the documented firmware and acquisition scope.

sections.heading: Install the development kit
sections.text: Install the development kit Start with the official ounce-devkit repository. Install devkitPro pacman using its own platform instructions, then use the versioned overlay: The installer can install missing packages and replace an existing libounce and portlibs/switch2 overlay. Review the pinned installer before updating an environment used by another project. Check the installed identity and build rules: If DEVKITPRO is not set in your shell, load the devkitPro environment for your installation. Do not substitute a guessed prefix into an existing project's configuration.

sections.heading: Build the smallest graphics example
sections.text: Build the smallest graphics example From the ounce-devkit repository, build its Vulkan clear example: The example clears a native window without shaders and uses Plus to exit. This isolates the surface, queue and presentation path from shader compilation and asset loading. Read the example source and retain the generated ELF and NRO. For an OpenGL ES starting point: Use a clean build directory when changing the target platform or development-kit version. OunceVK is linked statically, so a driver update requires rebuilding the application.

sections.heading: Run the native application
sections.text: Run the native application Once kaiHEN and hbmenu are running on a supported console, transfer the NRO to an application directory on SD, such as: That directory is a convention for organizing your app, not an access-control boundary. OunceShell's FTP service can transfer builds and retrieve logs in an existing environment. Open the application from hbmenu. Record whether a frame appears, whether controller input works and whether Plus returns to a usable menu. Repeat the launch, then open an unrelated application. These observations test different parts of the lifecycle.

sections.heading: Start your application
sections.text: Start your application Copy the reference example into your own project and update its target and NACP metadata. Keep the native rules include: For ordinary applications, -lnx then resolves through the libounce installation. Select the graphics library before the runtime: For an EGL/GLES application use -lEGL -lnx . A resident plugin has different startup and linking requirements; follow Plugins and IPC rather than changing an NRO's file extension.

sections.heading: Add features in a useful order
sections.text: Add features in a useful order Step Build Observe --- --- --- Native entry Status and a simple screen Startup result and a normal return Input One controller action Correct press edges and reconnect behavior Files Load one known asset Missing-file behavior and bounded reads Renderer One representative scene Correct output and repeated presentation Audio Short PCM output Buffer ownership and clean stop Optional systems Network, decoder, JIT or plugin Independent initialization and failure paths Keep portable logic runnable on the host. Use console tests to establish device behavior and host tests to validate parsers, protocols and deterministic algorithms.

sections.heading: If the first launch fails
sections.text: If the first launch fails If a native game opens instead of hbmenu, check the environment's policy/arming stage. If hbmenu warns about the NRO, check the target metadata and runtime library selection. If the app opens but no frame appears, log each graphics initialization call and its result. Continue with Build your first app for the original status diagnostic, then Debugging and testing for a subsystem-by-subsystem workflow.

title: kaiHEN API reference
description: Function signatures, ownership rules, protocol values and failure handling.

sections.heading: kaiHEN API reference
sections.text: kaiHEN API reference The client interface is declared in kaihen.h ; protocol layouts are in kaihen/protocol.h . Include the headers from the same pinned devkit you link against. This reference covers the inspected protocol version 6 interface. Client declarations · Protocol definitions

sections.heading: Open a homebrew session
sections.text: Open a homebrew session kaihenGetRoSession wraps the loader's borrowed ldr:ro session. The homebrew session opened through it is owned by the caller. Close that session after use; retain the loader's handle. This is an illustrative ownership pattern. Check transport results before reading output structures, and keep a UI or log path available when the optional HEN query fails.

sections.heading: Status fields
sections.text: Status fields Field Type Meaning --- --- --- process_id u64 The HEN process ID protocol_version u32 Implemented HEN homebrew protocol initialization_result Result HEN's startup result A successful henGetStatus means the request completed. Inspect the returned startup result independently. Use protocol checks to gate features rather than assuming all commands exist because the session opened.

sections.heading: Owned resource copies
sections.text: Owned resource copies These calls return owned handles for the documented resource or proxy. Their initialization and forwarding semantics differ. Use libounce's ordinary service paths wherever possible, and read Runtime and ABI before sending low-level initialization commands to an override. For every acquired resource, record whether it is borrowed, owned, initialized, active or already closed. In C++, a move-only wrapper can encode ownership. In C, a single unwind path with initialization flags keeps partially successful startup predictable.

sections.heading: Plugin discovery
sections.text: Plugin discovery Commands 20–22 provide plugin discovery and opening. A published name is the plugin filename without .nso . Opening creates a fresh owned client session; a plugin's own command protocol still needs separate version negotiation. Enumerate again after an unavailable result rather than trusting a cached process ID. A plugin may run without publishing a service, so an empty list does not prove no plugin processes exist. See Plugins and IPC for startup, readiness, payload limits and service shutdown.

sections.heading: Protocol command map
sections.text: Protocol command map Command Operation --- --- 0 Get status 16 Get filesystem root 17 Get settings session 18 Get caller process handle 19 Get service-manager proxy session 20 Get published plugin count 21 Get plugin name 22 Open plugin Use the public wrappers unless a concrete implementation gap requires raw IPC. Keep custom payloads fixed-width and validate sizes on both sides of the boundary.

sections.heading: JIT entry points
sections.text: JIT entry points Native applications use libounce's Jit interface and link the kaiHEN provider with -lkaihen : Emit into jitGetRwAddr and execute through jitGetRxAddr only after successful publication and the required synchronization. The application-visible RW buffer is staging, so direct writes do not independently publish new executable bytes. Sparse publication uses kaihenJitPublishRanges . JIT provider guide · JIT runtime implementation See JIT and language runtimes before integrating an emitter that assumes a directly coherent writable alias.

sections.heading: Failure handling
sections.text: Failure handling Log the API name and hexadecimal Result immediately. Read outputs only after success. Keep transport failure separate from a nonzero result embedded in a reply. Clean up only resources that were actually acquired. For a mutating plugin command, a timeout can leave the outcome uncertain. Add a request identifier and a status operation before enabling retries. A documentation example that omits application-specific recovery is not a complete retry policy.

sections.heading: Version scope
sections.text: Version scope The research snapshot describes concrete source revisions, not an automatically refreshed ABI contract. Review upstream changes when adopting a new devkit, rebuild static dependencies and run the relevant lifecycle tests. Source declarations and host fixtures do not establish universal console behavior.

sections.heading: MCP integration
sections.text: MCP integration Use the documentation from your development tools through the same source-backed corpus that powers this site. The public endpoint supports read-only search, topic retrieval and source lookup.

sections.heading: Connection URL
sections.text: Connection URL Add this URL as a remote HTTP MCP server in a compatible client. No API key or account is required for these public documents. Each request is independent; the service stores no chat history and has no access to your console, workspace or local credentials. The endpoint supports MCP 2026-07-28 and a stateless compatibility path for earlier HTTP clients. It uses the MCP SDK v2 and the Cloudflare Workers handler. Legacy standalone SSE connections and resumable sessions are not offered.

sections.text: Available tools Tool Inputs Result --- --- --- search query , optional limit Ranked sections with IDs, excerpts and canonical links fetch id Full page or section Markdown with evidence dates and source URLs list_docs Optional group Topic index with descriptions get_sources id Source references for the topic The server also exposes documentation pages as Markdown resources. All tools are declared read-only and return the site's published documentation. They do not acquire a homebrew environment, run builds or perform filesystem operations.

sections.heading: Search, then retrieve
sections.text: Search, then retrieve Start with a specific subsystem or API name: Use a returned section ID with fetch : Document IDs such as toolchain return the whole guide. Canonical documentation URLs are accepted as well. get_sources returns the underlying references so a client can preserve citations while explaining an API or recommending a change.

Ask the client to preserve the research date and distinguish a declared API from hardware-tested behavior. The server cannot add evidence of a test that has not been run.

sections.text: Test an HTTP connection For a basic compatibility-path check, send an initialization request: A successful response includes the server identity and negotiated protocol. A compatible client normally handles negotiation for you. Use POST for MCP requests; opening /mcp in a browser address bar is a GET request and is not a connection test. If a connection fails, verify the URL, HTTP transport support and the client's negotiation output. A browser-origin rejection is distinct from a missing document or a tool argument error.
